I10.overview: A condition characterised by elevated blood pressure measured on 3 separate occasions, a minimum of 2 days apart: systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg and/or diastolic BP ≥ 90 mmHg.

Maintain ideal weight

B20.overview: HIV is a retrovirus that attacks the immune system (CD4 lymphocytes). Without treatment it progresses to AIDS. All PLHIV are eligible for ART regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage.

emergencyProtocol.outcome: Most HIV-related emergencies need hospital referral.

specialCases.note: Initiate ART immediately with TLD.
Start TB first. CD4 <50: ART within 2 weeks; CD4 ≥50: defer 8 weeks.
Defer ART 8 weeks.
Defer ART 4-6 weeks after starting antifungals.

A15.overview: TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Spreads through the air. DS-TB is treated with a 6-month regimen: 2 months RHZE + 4 months RH.

medications.name: RH — Rifampicin + Isoniazid

medications.name: Pyridoxine

Do not stop even if you feel better

Open windows, let in sunlight
Eat well; stop smoking; limit alcohol
Attend every follow-up

All first-line drugs safe. Give pyridoxine.

J45.overview: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways. Exposure to triggers causes inflammation, bronchospasm, and increased mucus. Asthma cannot be cured but can be well-controlled. Most treatment failures are due to poor inhaler technique or poor adherence.

High-dose ICS + reliever; escalate to LABA/ICS

medications.name: Salbutamol (Reliever)
medications.notes: Immediate relief. Increasing use = not controlled.

medications.name: Beclomethasone (Controller)
medications.frequency: Step 1: 200 mcg with each salbutamol. Step 2: 200 mcg twice daily. Step 3: 400 mcg twice daily

medications.frequency: Step 2: 200 mcg twice daily. Step 3: 400 mcg twice daily

inhalerTechnique.mdi:
1. Remove cap and shake.
2. Breathe out gently.
3. Seal lips around mouthpiece.
4. Press canister and breathe in slowly (3–5 sec).
5. Hold breath 10 sec.
6. Wait 30 sec between puffs.
7. Rinse mouth after steroid inhaler.
inhalerTechnique.spacer:
1. Shake inhaler, insert into spacer.
2. Seal lips around mouthpiece.
3. Press canister ONCE.
4. Breathe in and out slowly 5–6 times.
5. Wait 30 sec between puffs.
6. Wash spacer weekly, air-dry.
generalTips: Always shake the inhaler before use.
Use a spacer for all children and adults on Step 3.
Rinse mouth after using a preventer inhaler.

specialCases.note: Diagnosis difficult — refer all.
Use beclomethasone, not budesonide or fluticasone.

A09.overview: Sudden onset of loose stools with or without vomiting. Usually viral; may be bacterial or parasitic. Most cases self-limiting. Dehydration is the main danger — especially in children.
A09.treatmentDurationText: Usually resolves in 3–7 days with correct rehydration

medications.name: Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)
medications.dosage: Plan B: 80 mL/kg over 4 h. Plan A: 10 mL/kg after each stool
medications.notes: Cup-and-spoon method. If vomiting, wait 10 min, continue slowly.

medications.name: Homemade SSS
medications.dosage: ½ tsp salt + 8 tsp sugar in 1 L boiled/cooled water
medications.notes: Discard after 24 hours.

medications.name: Zinc — children
medications.notes: Give zinc to ALL children with acute diarrhoea.

medications.name: Loperamide — adults
medications.dosage: 4 mg initially, then 2 mg after each stool
medications.notes: NOT for children. NOT for bloody diarrhoea.

medications.name: Ceftriaxone (before referral)
medications.phase: Neonates with severe dehydration OR children with SAM
medications.notes: Only before referral in high-risk groups.

lifestyleAdvice: Keep giving ORS/SSS even if patient vomits
Continue feeding
Give small frequent meals
Give zinc to children for 14 full days
Wash hands with soap
Boil drinking water if unsure
Return IMMEDIATELY if warning signs
A09.followUpSchedule: Return immediately if: no improvement, poor drinking, blood in stool, fever, sunken eyes. Follow up in 5 days if diarrhoea persists.

emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Ringers lactate or NaCl 0.9% IV, 20 mL/kg rapidly. If SAM: 10 mL/kg over 10 min. Repeat up to twice if weak pulse. Continue 20 mL/kg hourly × 5 h. Give ORS as soon as child can drink. Refer urgently.

specialCases.note: Consider dysentery — refer.
Give ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg before referral.
Reduce IV bolus to 10 mL/kg. Give ceftriaxone before referral.

A09.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 2, Sections 2.9.1 and 2.9.3

B54.overview: Malaria is an infection of red blood cells by a Plasmodium parasite, transmitted by the bite of an infected mosquito. In South Africa, P. falciparum is the most common and most dangerous species. Symptoms are non-specific: fever, severe headache, shivering, nausea/vomiting, flu-like symptoms, muscle/joint pains, diarrhoea. Any person resident in or returning from a malaria area with fever should be tested for malaria. Progression to severe disease can be rapid, so early diagnosis and treatment is critical.
phases: Diagnose — thick and thin blood smears OR rapid diagnostic test (HRP2)
First dose — give artemether/lumefantrine under supervision, observe for 1 hour
Monitor for severe malaria signs during the first 24 hours

medications.name: Artemether/lumefantrine 20/120 mg
medications.frequency: First dose immediately, second 8 hours later, then 12-hourly for 2 more days (6 doses total)
medications.notes: MUST take with fat-containing food or full cream milk to ensure adequate absorption. Give the FIRST DOSE UNDER SUPERVISION at the clinic — observe for at least 1 hour as vomiting is common. If the patient vomits within the first hour, repeat the dose. Vomiting oral treatment is one of the most common reasons for treatment failure.

medications.name: Paracetamol — for fever
medications.dosage: Children <5 years: 10–15 mg/kg/dose. Adults: 500 mg to 1 g
medications.notes: For fever management. Maximum 4 g in 24 hours for adults.

lifestyleAdvice: Take all 6 doses of artemether/lumefantrine — do not stop early even if you feel better
Always take each dose WITH fatty food or full cream milk — this is essential for the medicine to work
If you vomit within 1 hour of a dose, go back to the clinic and get another dose
Use mosquito nets impregnated with insecticide (DEET)
Apply insect repellent (30% DEET) to exposed skin and clothing
Wear long sleeves, long trousers and socks outdoors between dusk and dawn
Get a second malaria test if symptoms continue after treatment
One negative test does not exclude malaria — ask for a second test if still unwell
Pregnant women, children under 5, and people with HIV are at high risk of severe malaria — seek care early

duringTreatment: Observe patient for at least 1 hour after first dose for vomiting
Monitor for severe malaria signs during the first 24 hours
followUp: If no improvement at 48 hours, refer for evaluation
If symptoms persist or recur after treatment, do a repeat blood smear

All patients presenting to PHC clinics in areas that do not stock antimalarials
Vomiting leading to inability to retain medication
Patients not responding to oral treatment within 48 hours
After first dose of artemether/lumefantrine, refer: all children <2 years, all pregnant women, patients with co-morbidities (HIV, diabetes etc.), and patients >65 years

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Any sign of severe/complicated malaria (prostration, coma, convulsions, respiratory distress, jaundice, renal failure, shock, black urine, severe anaemia)
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Correct hypoglycaemia if present. Give artesunate IM (see B50 — severe malaria). Refer urgently. Patient must reach referral hospital within 6 hours of being seen at the PHC facility.

specialCases.note: After first dose of artemether/lumefantrine, refer for observation — they are at high risk of severe malaria.
After first dose, refer urgently. High risk of severe malaria.

Higher risk. Refer after first dose.

Does NOT exclude the diagnosis. Request a 2nd test if clinical suspicion is high.

B54.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 10, Section 10.7.1

B50.overview: Severe malaria is a medical emergency with high mortality. Any patient with confirmed or suspected malaria who presents with prostration, altered consciousness, convulsions, respiratory distress, jaundice, renal failure, shock, repeated vomiting, hypoglycaemia, severe anaemia (Hb <7 g/dL), haemoglobinuria (black urine), or abnormal bleeding has severe malaria. Requires IMMEDIATE treatment with IV/IM artesunate and URGENT referral — patient must reach referral hospital within 6 hours.
B50.treatmentDurationText: Acute emergency — immediate artesunate + urgent referral

severityLevels.systolic: Any one of: prostration, sleepiness, coma, convulsions, respiratory distress, cyanosis, jaundice, renal failure, shock, repeated vomiting, hypoglycaemia, Hb <7 g/dL, black urine, abnormal bleeding

phases: Step 1 — Recognise severe malaria (any one sign)
Step 2 — Correct hypoglycaemia immediately if present
Step 4 — Refer urgently to hospital within 6 hours

medications.name: Artesunate IM — adults and children ≥20 kg
medications.frequency: Immediately as a single dose, then refer. If transfer is delayed, repeat at 12 hours and 24 hours
medications.notes: Reconstitution: 60 mg vial + 1 mL sodium bicarbonate, shake well, then add 5 mL sodium chloride 0.9% → final concentration 10 mg/mL. Administer as IM injection (anterior thigh). Correct hypoglycaemia BEFORE giving artesunate. Patient must reach referral hospital within 6 hours of being seen at the PHC facility.

medications.name: Artesunate IM — children <20 kg
medications.frequency: Immediately as a single dose, then refer. If transfer is delayed, repeat at 12 hours and 24 hours
medications.notes: Higher mg/kg dose for children <20 kg. Same reconstitution as adults. Correct hypoglycaemia first. Refer urgently.

lifestyleAdvice: This is a medical emergency — treatment must begin immediately
Do not delay referral — patient must reach hospital within 6 hours
Correct low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) BEFORE giving artesunate
If transfer is delayed, additional doses of artesunate are given at 12 and 24 hours
Tell the referral hospital that the initial artesunate dose has been given
Do not give oral medicines — the patient is too unwell to absorb them
Keep the patient warm, monitor breathing and consciousness during transport

beforeReferral: Check blood glucose — correct hypoglycaemia immediately
Monitor respiratory rate and oxygen saturation
duringTransfer: Keep patient on their side if unconscious

B50.followUpSchedule: Handover to referral hospital. Complete treatment there. Do not delay transfer.
referralCriteria: All patients — severe malaria is always a hospital referral
Refer within 6 hours of first contact — this is critical
Patient must be transported by ambulance if possible
Advise referral hospital that initial artesunate has been given

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Any sign of severe malaria (prostration, coma, convulsions, respiratory distress, jaundice, renal failure, shock, black urine, severe anaemia, abnormal bleeding)
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: 1. Correct hypoglycaemia immediately if present (dextrose 10% IV, 2–5 mL/kg). 2. Give artesunate IM — 2.4 mg/kg (adults and children ≥20 kg) OR 3 mg/kg (children <20 kg). 3. Refer urgently to hospital — must arrive within 6 hours. 4. If transfer delayed: repeat artesunate at 12 hours and 24 hours. 5. Advise referral hospital that artesunate was given.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Life-threatening — 100% of cases must be referred urgently. Do NOT delay for observation.

specialCases.note: Use 3 mg/kg per dose (not 2.4 mg/kg). Higher dose needed because of lower body water content.
Correct immediately before giving artesunate. Hypoglycaemia is common in severe malaria and can cause coma.
If transfer is delayed, administer additional artesunate doses at 12 hours and 24 hours.
60 mg vial + 1 mL sodium bicarbonate → shake → add 5 mL NaCl 0.9% → final 10 mg/mL. Use immediately after reconstitution.
Artesunate is the treatment of choice in all trimesters of pregnancy — do not withhold. Refer urgently.

B50.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 10, Section 10.7.2

F32.9.overview: Depression is more than just feeling sad. It is a real medical condition where your thoughts and behaviour are driven by a low mood that doesn't go away. It can affect how you think, feel, sleep, eat, and function day-to-day. Depression is common, treatable, and NOT a sign of weakness. It is often not recognized — by the person experiencing it or by health workers — because of stigma or because it shows up as physical symptoms (headaches, body aches, tiredness) rather than sadness. Depression can affect anyone, at any age, and often goes together with other medical conditions (like HIV, TB, diabetes, or chronic pain).
F32.9.treatmentDurationText: Continue treatment for at least 9 months after symptoms improve — sometimes longer (up to 3 years or lifelong) depending on history

severityLevels.systolic: Some symptoms present, but you can still do most daily tasks
severityLevels.diastolic: Psychotherapy (talk therapy) is usually the first choice. Medicines may not be needed yet.

severityLevels.systolic: Symptoms make daily tasks harder — work, family, and self-care affected
severityLevels.diastolic: Combination of psychotherapy (if available) OR antidepressant medication

severityLevels.systolic: Symptoms interfere with nearly everything — you may feel unable to function
severityLevels.diastolic: Medication is essential. Psychotherapy recommended alongside. Refer if psychotic features or suicidal thoughts.

phases: Recognise the signs — low mood and/or loss of interest for at least 2 weeks
Rule out other medical causes — HIV, TB, anaemia, thyroid problems, substance use
Offer choice of treatment — talk therapy (if available) or antidepressant medicine
Start medicine slowly — fluoxetine 20 mg on alternate days for the first 2 weeks
Increase to daily dose after 2–4 weeks — monitor for agitation or worsening mood
Reassess response after 4 weeks on daily fluoxetine
Continue treatment for 9 months minimum after you feel better — do NOT stop early
Follow up regularly — weekly contact for the first 2 months if risk of self-harm is present

medications.name: Fluoxetine (first-line antidepressant)
medications.dosage: 20 mg (start with alternate days for the first 2 weeks, then daily)
medications.duration: Minimum 9 months after symptoms improve — longer if history of previous episodes
medications.notes: IMPORTANT: Doctors prescribe this. You may notice increased anxiety or restlessness in the first 2–4 weeks — this usually settles. It can take 2–4 weeks to notice any improvement — don't give up too early. If you have thoughts of harming yourself, tell your CHW or go to the clinic IMMEDIATELY — you may need to be referred before starting this medicine. Do NOT stop suddenly — always reduce slowly with your doctor. Do NOT take St John's Wort or traditional medicines with this — they can interact dangerously.

medications.name: Citalopram (alternative antidepressant)
medications.dosage: 10 mg daily for the first week, then increase to 20 mg daily
medications.notes: Another antidepressant in the same family (SSRI). Same precautions about agitation in the first few weeks and monitoring for suicidal thoughts. Doctor-prescribed.

medications.name: Amitriptyline (if a sedating antidepressant is needed)
medications.dosage: 25 mg at bedtime, increase by 25 mg every 3–5 days up to a maximum of 150 mg per day
medications.phase: Only if a sedating effect is needed (e.g. severe insomnia)
medications.notes: This is a tricyclic antidepressant. It can be FATAL in overdose — must be kept out of reach of children and anyone at risk of self-harm. Doctor-prescribed only, and requires a risk assessment of the patient and others in the household (especially adolescents). NOT for elderly patients or those with heart disease, urinary retention, glaucoma, or epilepsy.

lifestyleAdvice: You are not alone — depression is common, treatable, and not your fault
Talk to someone you trust — a friend, family member, or your CHW
Stay connected — isolation makes depression worse, even when it feels easier
Keep a simple routine — wake up and go to bed at the same time each day
Move your body — even a short walk helps lift mood
Eat regularly — depression often affects appetite
Avoid alcohol and drugs — they make depression worse and interact badly with medicines
Set small, achievable goals — big tasks feel overwhelming
Be patient with yourself — recovery takes time
Take your medicine every day, even when you feel better — stopping early causes relapse
Attend every appointment — your CHW needs to check on you regularly
If you have thoughts of harming yourself — tell someone immediately, call a helpline, or go to the nearest clinic
SADAG helpline (SA Depression and Anxiety Group) — 0800 456 789 (toll-free, 24/7)
Lifeline South Africa — 0861 322 322
Family and friends — let them help, even with small things

everyVisit: Ask about mood — how have you been feeling?
Ask about sleep, appetite, energy levels
Ask directly about thoughts of self-harm or suicide — this is essential
Check whether you are taking your medicine regularly
Ask about side effects of medicine
baseline: Rule out medical causes — HIV test, TB screen, anaemia (Hb), thyroid function, blood glucose
Screen for substance use (alcohol, cannabis, benzodiazepines)
Assess severity — mild, moderate, or severe
Ask specifically about suicidal thoughts, plans, and access to means
Ask about psychosocial stressors — abuse, financial problems, relationship issues, bereavement
followUp: Weekly contact for the first 2 months if any risk of self-harm is present
Reassess symptoms at 4 weeks after starting daily medicine
If no improvement after 8 weeks on the correct dose — refer to doctor
Reassess at every visit for suicidal thoughts

F32.9.followUpSchedule: Weekly contact for the first 2 months if any risk of self-harm is present. Reassess response to medicine at 4 weeks. If no improvement at 8 weeks despite correct medicine and dose, refer to doctor. Continue treatment for at least 9 months after symptoms improve.
warningSigns: Thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life
Feeling that life is not worth living
Making a plan to harm yourself
Giving away possessions or saying goodbye to loved ones
Severe agitation or restlessness (especially in the first few weeks of medicine)
Sudden worsening of mood after starting medicine
Hearing voices or seeing things others don't see (psychosis)
Unable to care for yourself or dependent children
Alcohol or drug use getting worse
referralCriteria: Any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life — refer IMMEDIATELY
Major depression with psychotic features (hearing voices, seeing things, delusions)
Suspected bipolar disorder (history of manic or hypomanic episodes)
Failure to respond to antidepressant after 8 weeks on the correct dose
Children and adolescents with depression — refer to specialist
Severe depression with inability to function
Access to lethal means (weapons, pesticides, large quantities of medication)

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Any thoughts of self-harm, suicide, or imminent risk (patient is extremely agitated, distressed, or has a current plan)
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: DO NOT leave the person alone. Remove access to means (bleach, pesticides, firearms, medications, especially paracetamol, amitriptyline, theophylline). Stay with them until help arrives. Refer IMMEDIATELY to hospital — do not send them alone. If a serious act of self-harm has already occurred, treat as a medical emergency first (see Section 21.3 — Trauma and injuries).
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Suicidal ideation is a medical emergency. Never delay referral. Never dismiss or minimise.

specialCases.note: ASK about suicidal thoughts at every visit — especially in adolescents and young adults. Antidepressants can occasionally increase suicidal thoughts in the first few weeks. If they are present, refer to hospital before continuing treatment.
Higher risk of suicidal ideation during early treatment. Monitor closely. Refer all adolescents to a specialist.
Refer to a doctor. Untreated depression is dangerous for both mother and baby, but medicine must be carefully chosen.
Do NOT give antidepressants alone — they can trigger a manic episode. If there is any history of mania or hypomania, refer to a specialist.
Alcohol and drug use makes depression worse and interferes with treatment. Address substance use at the same time as depression.
Depression makes chronic diseases (HIV, TB, diabetes, heart disease) harder to manage. Treating depression improves outcomes for these conditions too.
Some traditional medicines and St John's Wort interact dangerously with antidepressants. Ask about them before starting medicine.
Most relapses happen because people stop treatment as soon as they feel better. Continue treatment for the full duration (minimum 9 months) even when you feel fine.

F32.9.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 16, Sections 16.4 and 16.4.1 (Mood disorders — Depressive disorders) and Section 16.7 (Suicide risk assessment)

J18.9.overview: Pneumonia is an acute infection of the lung tissue, usually caused by bacteria — most commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus). It causes the air sacs in the lungs to fill with fluid or pus, making it hard to breathe. Symptoms include fever (often with sudden onset and shivering), cough (may be dry at first, then productive of yellow-green or rusty-brown sputum), chest pain that worsens on breathing in, and shortness of breath. Older adults may not have a fever but can present with confusion. Pneumonia can occur in previously healthy people or as a complication of another illness. HIV, malnutrition, very young or old age, and chronic diseases increase the risk.
J18.9.treatmentDurationText: 5 days of antibiotics — review at 48 hours if no improvement
phases: Diagnose — clinical signs (fever, cough, tachypnoea, crackles) + chest X-ray if available
Exclude TB — send sputum for TB-NAAT (GeneXpert)
Assess severity — uncomplicated vs with underlying conditions vs severe
Start antibiotics — amoxicillin (or amoxicillin/clavulanic acid if underlying conditions)
Review at 48 hours — refer if no response
Complete 5-day course — follow-up X-ray if >50 years

medications.name: Amoxicillin — uncomplicated pneumonia (adults)
medications.notes: First-line for uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia in adults. If not severely ill and no underlying conditions, this can be managed at PHC level. Review at 48 hours — refer if no improvement. Chest X-ray ideally before starting treatment.

medications.name: Amoxicillin/clavulanic acid — pneumonia with underlying conditions (adults)
medications.phase: Adults — with underlying medical conditions or >65 years
medications.notes: For patients with diabetes, alcoholism, HIV, cardiac failure, chronic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, or COPD. Most of these patients will require referral to a doctor.

medications.name: Moxifloxacin — penicillin allergy alternative
medications.notes: Use ONLY if severe penicillin allergy (Z88.0). Reserved antibiotic — do NOT use as first-line. Doctor-prescribed.

medications.name: Ceftriaxone — severe pneumonia before referral
medications.notes: Give ONLY to patients with severe pneumonia (≥2 of: confusion, RR ≥30, age >65, SBP <90, DBP <60) — before urgent referral. Do NOT give calcium-containing IV fluids (like Ringer Lactate) with ceftriaxone. Also give oxygen to keep saturation 92%.

medications.name: Amoxicillin — non-severe pneumonia in children
medications.notes: Children with pneumonia (fever, cough, rapid breathing) but NO chest indrawing and NO flaring nostrils. See weight-band table. Give to a child who is drinking well and has no danger signs.

weightBands.dose: 250 mg (5 mL of 250/5mL syrup OR 10 mL of 125/5mL)
375 mg (7.5 mL of 250/5mL OR 15 mL of 125/5mL)
500 mg (2 × 250 mg capsules OR 1 × 500 mg capsule)
1000 mg (4 × 250 mg capsules OR 2 × 500 mg capsules)
1500 mg (6 × 250 mg capsules OR 3 × 500 mg capsules)

medications.name: Azithromycin — severe penicillin allergy in children
medications.notes: Use ONLY if severe penicillin allergy. See dosing table Chapter 23.

medications.name: Ceftriaxone — severe pneumonia in children before referral
medications.notes: Give to children with severe pneumonia (chest indrawing, flaring nostrils, or grunting) before urgent referral. Do NOT inject more than 1 g per injection site. Give oxygen via nasal cannula at 1–2 L/min before and during transfer.

medications.name: Oxygen — severe pneumonia
medications.notes: Adults: 92% saturation target. Children: nasal cannula at 1–2 L/min before and during transfer.

lifestyleAdvice: Take the full course of antibiotics — do not stop even if you feel better
Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Do not smoke — it delays recovery
Cover your mouth when you cough
Wash your hands frequently to prevent spread
Return to the clinic if symptoms get worse or don't improve after 48 hours
If you have children in the house, keep them away from your cough
Get the flu vaccine annually, especially if you have underlying conditions
If you have a chronic illness (diabetes, HIV, COPD), keep it well-controlled — it reduces pneumonia risk

everyVisit: Check for confusion or reduced consciousness
baseline: Chest X-ray if available — ideally in all patients
Sputum TB-NAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF) — to exclude TB
followUp: Review at 48 hours — refer if no improvement
Follow-up chest X-ray in patients >50 years to ensure resolution

J18.9.followUpSchedule: Review at 48 hours. If no improvement, refer urgently. Chest X-ray follow-up in patients >50 years to ensure resolution. Complete 5 days of antibiotics.
warningSigns: Confusion or decreased level of consciousness
No improvement after 48 hours of treatment
referralCriteria: Any of: confusion, cyanosis, RR ≥ 30, SBP < 90, DBP < 60
No response to treatment after 48 hours
Patients from a poor socio-economic background
Patients unlikely to comply with treatment
Patients living a considerable distance from health centres
Patients with no access to immediate transport
All children with severe pneumonia (chest indrawing, flaring nostrils, or cyanosis)
All children < 2 months of age with rapid breathing
Pneumonia in patients with underlying conditions (diabetes, HIV, cardiac failure, CLD, CKD, COPD) — most require referral

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Severe pneumonia (≥2 of: confusion, RR ≥30, age >65, SBP <90, DBP <60) OR any danger sign in children
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Adults: oxygen to keep saturation 92%. Give ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM single dose before referral. Children: oxygen via nasal cannula 1–2 L/min. Give ceftriaxone IM 80 mg/kg (do not exceed 1 g per injection site) before urgent referral. Do NOT give calcium-containing IV fluids (Ringer Lactate) with ceftriaxone.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Severe pneumonia is life-threatening — refer urgently to hospital.

specialCases.note: Any rapid breathing (≥60 breaths/minute) should be classified as severe pneumonia — refer immediately.
Higher risk of severe pneumonia and complications. Lower threshold for referral.
Higher risk. Even mild symptoms can deteriorate quickly. Refer if any underlying condition present.

specialCases.case: Patients with diabetes, alcoholism, HIV, cardiac failure, chronic liver or kidney disease, COPD
specialCases.note: Use amoxicillin/clavulanic acid instead of plain amoxicillin. Most require referral to a doctor.
Use moxifloxacin 400 mg daily × 5 days (adults) or azithromycin 10 mg/kg daily × 3 days (children).
Consider TB — send sputum for TB-NAAT. Also consider resistant organisms or complications (empyema, abscess).
See B20.6 for HIV-related Pneumocystis pneumonia — treated with high-dose cotrimoxazole, not amoxicillin.

J18.9.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Sections 17.3.4.2.1 (Uncomplicated pneumonia), 17.3.4.2.2 (With underlying conditions), 17.3.4.2.3 (Severe pneumonia), and 17.3.4.1 (Children)

B20.6.conditionName: HIV disease resulting in Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)
B20.6.overview: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is a serious lung infection caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jiroveci. It occurs almost exclusively in people with advanced HIV infection (usually CD4 count <200 cells/mm³) and in other severely immunocompromised patients. PCP causes inflammation and fluid buildup in the air sacs of the lungs, making it hard to breathe. Symptoms typically develop gradually over days to weeks and include shortness of breath (especially on exertion), a dry cough, and sometimes fever. In early stages, the chest X-ray may look normal. Prompt treatment is essential — PCP can be life-threatening if not treated early. Patients with PCP also need to be started on ART (see B20).
B20.6.treatmentDurationText: 3 weeks of cotrimoxazole treatment, followed by long-term daily prophylaxis
phases: Diagnose — symptoms (shortness of breath, dry cough) + HIV+ with low CD4 + chest X-ray findings
Treat for 3 weeks — complete full course
Start ART — usually during PCP treatment (see B20)
Secondary prophylaxis — cotrimoxazole daily after acute treatment
Stop prophylaxis — when CD4 >200 for at least 6 months

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole — acute PCP treatment
medications.notes: High-dose cotrimoxazole is the first-line treatment for PCP. Can cause rash, nausea, bone marrow suppression, and hyperkalaemia. Monitor closely. Always ensure adequate hydration. Refer ALL children with PCP — do not treat at PHC level.

weightBands.dose: 2 tablets of 160/800 mg (or 4 tablets of 80/400 mg) 6-hourly
3 tablets of 160/800 mg (or 6 tablets of 80/400 mg) 6-hourly
4 tablets of 160/800 mg (or 8 tablets of 80/400 mg) 6-hourly

medications.name: Cotrimoxazole — secondary prophylaxis (after acute treatment)
medications.dosage: 160/800 mg (double-strength tablet) OR 2 tablets of 80/400 mg
medications.duration: Until CD4 >200 cells/mm³ for at least 6 months on ART
medications.notes: After completing 3 weeks of high-dose treatment, continue cotrimoxazole once daily to prevent recurrence. Discontinue ONLY once the CD4 count has been above 200 for at least 6 months on ART. If the patient develops a rash with fever, mucosal involvement, or facial swelling — stop immediately and refer.

medications.name: Oxygen
medications.notes: Give oxygen if oxygen saturation <90%. Refer if breathing rate >24 breaths/minute, shortness of breath on mild effort, or cyanosis.

lifestyleAdvice: Take every dose of cotrimoxazole — this medicine cures the infection
Attend every follow-up appointment — PCP can come back if you stop treatment too early
Start ART as soon as the doctor prescribes it — this protects your immune system and prevents recurrence
Report any new rash, fever, or shortness of breath immediately
Drink plenty of water while on cotrimoxazole
Avoid smoking — it worsens lung damage
Wear a mask in crowded places until your immune system recovers
Get the flu vaccine annually
If you have children, keep them away from your cough until you are no longer infectious
SADAG helpline (if you feel depressed or overwhelmed) — 0800 456 789

baseline: Chest X-ray — typically shows bilateral interstitial or ground glass pattern (may be normal early)
Full blood count (cotrimoxazole can suppress bone marrow)
HIV viral load if not recent
duringTreatment: Assess response within the first week
Monitor for adverse drug reactions (rash, anaemia, hyperkalaemia)
Ensure ART is started appropriately (see B20 for timing)

B20.6.followUpSchedule: Review within the first week of treatment. Ensure 3-week course completed. Start ART during treatment (usually within 2 weeks — see B20 for timing). Continue secondary prophylaxis daily until CD4 >200 for at least 6 months. Reassess at every ART refill.
warningSigns: Shortness of breath with mild effort
New rash with fever or mucosal involvement (cotrimoxazole hypersensitivity)
Extreme fatigue or pallor (bone marrow suppression)
referralCriteria: Shortness of breath with mild effort
Confusion or reduced level of consciousness
Suspected cotrimoxazole hypersensitivity (rash with systemic features or mucosal involvement)
Failure to respond to treatment after 1 week
Severe anaemia or hyperkalaemia during treatment

emergencyProtocol.trigger: Severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, or altered consciousness in a patient with PCP
emergencyProtocol.immediateAction: Give oxygen to keep saturation above 90%. Refer IMMEDIATELY to hospital — do NOT delay. Continue cotrimoxazole if already started. Ensure IV access. Monitor breathing continuously during transfer.
emergencyProtocol.outcome: Severe PCP is life-threatening — refer urgently.

specialCases.note: Refer ALL children with PCP — do not treat at PHC level. Paediatric PCP is a hospital-level emergency.
Cotrimoxazole is safe in pregnancy (particularly in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters). Refer for specialist review. Untreated PCP is more dangerous than the medicine.

If there is a history of severe sulphonamide (cotrimoxazole) allergy, PCP treatment requires an alternative regimen (pentamidine, clindamycin-primaquine, or atovaquone) which is only available at hospital level — refer urgently.
ART should be started as soon as feasible during PCP treatment — usually within 2 weeks. See B20 for full HIV management. Early ART reduces risk of further opportunistic infections.
Do NOT stop cotrimoxazole prophylaxis until CD4 >200 for at least 6 months on ART. Stopping early causes relapse of PCP.
Rash is common. STOP immediately and refer if systemic features (fever, mucosal involvement, facial swelling) develop.
All PLHIV with CD4 <200 cells/mm³ should receive cotrimoxazole prophylaxis BEFORE they develop PCP. See Z29.2 — HIV prophylaxis.

B20.6.source: SA PHC Standard Treatment Guidelines 2024, Chapter 17, Section 17.3.4.2.4 (Pneumocystis pneumonia) and Chapter 11 (HIV)
